screens.title: Welcome
screens.text: This app prepares you for the COS212 lecture on AVL trees. In about an hour, split into nine short lessons, you’ll see why a binary search tree can become slow, how an AVL tree keeps itself balanced, and how search, rotations and insertion work. Everything here is private practice: nothing is marked.

screens.title: Your route
screens.text: You can stop between lessons and pick up where you left off.
points: C1 Getting started and a quick readiness check
C2 When BSTs go lopsided
C3 The AVL property
C4 Search: the algorithm
C5 Rotations
C6 Insertion with rebalancing
C7 Deletion with rebalancing (optional)
C8 Choosing a structure
C9 Am I ready for the lecture?
objectives: Explain how AVL trees fix the problem of lopsided BSTs (LO1).
Calculate heights and balance factors and decide whether a tree is an AVL tree (LO2).
Trace a search in an AVL tree and explain why it takes O(log n) steps (LO3).
Choose and perform the rotation(s) that restore balance (LO4).
Insert keys into an AVL tree and rebalance it (LO5).
Judge when an AVL tree is a good choice, and why (LO6).
Delete a leaf and restore the AVL property (LO7, optional).

screens.title: How the app works
points: Next and Back are always in the same place. Replay shows the current step again.
Show the rule opens the written rule for the screen you are on.
Hint tells you what a question checks and which idea it relies on.
With each answer, tap Sure or Not sure. It helps the app spot ideas that need another look.
Practice tasks allow as many tries as you like. Check questions allow one re-attempt.
After each check you get a title, from Structural Savant to Complexity Cadet, and a suggested next step. You always decide where to go.
Any lesson you have completed can be opened again from the lesson list.

screens.title: The conventions card
screens.text: These are the conventions from the COS212 slides. The card is always available from the menu.
points: Height: the number of edges on the longest path from a node down to a leaf. A leaf has height 0; an empty branch has height −1.
Balance factor: bf = h(right) − h(left). Valid values are −1, 0 and +1. Negative means the left branch is taller.
The unbalanced node is called n, with children n.left and n.right.
Case 1 (LL), Case 2 (LR), Case 3 (RL) and Case 4 (RR) name where a new key went below n.
O(lg n) and O(log n) mean the same thing.
screens.caption: Node 20: bf = 1 − 0 = +1. Node 40: bf = 0 − 0 = 0. Each leaf: bf = −1 − (−1) = 0.

screens.title: The BST rule
screens.text: In a binary search tree, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller than the node, and every key in its right subtree is larger. Every subtree is itself a BST.
screens.caption: 5 is the root. 3 and 1 are smaller, so they are on the left. 7, 6 and 9 are larger, so they are on the right.

screens.title: Searching a BST
screens.text: Start at the root. Compare the key with the node: equal, stop; smaller, go left; larger, go right.

screens.title: Inserting into a BST
screens.text: Search for the new key. It goes in the empty branch where the search ends, so it always becomes a leaf.
steps: 4 goes in the empty right branch of 3.
Every node has a balance factor of −1, 0 or +1.

screens.title: Tree terms and height
points: The root has no parent. A leaf has no children. Nodes with the same parent are siblings.
The height of a node is the number of edges on the longest path down to a leaf.
Here the leaves 1, 6 and 9 have height 0, nodes 3 and 7 have height 1, and the root 5 has height 2.

task.stem: 8 is about to be inserted. Click the node that 8 becomes a child of.
task.hint: This checks BST insertion: search for the new key, and it goes in the empty branch where the search ends.

wrongAnswers.feedback: 7 already has a right child (9), so the search continues: 8 < 9, so 8 goes in the empty left branch of 9.

feedback.correct: 8 > 5: go right. 8 > 7: go right. 8 < 9: go left. The left branch of 9 is empty, so 8 becomes the left child of 9.
feedback.incorrect: 8 > 5: go right. 8 > 7: go right. 8 < 9: go left. The left branch of 9 is empty, so 8 becomes the left child of 9.
